content: The Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine is a live vaccine derived from an attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis. It was first developed by Calmette and Guérin at the Pasteur Institute in Lille, France, and was administered to humans for the first time in 1921. Over time, various BCG vaccine strains have been developed worldwide, and these strains differ in their characteristics, immune response induction, and tuberculin reactivity. These differences are attributed to genetic changes in the bacterial strains and variations in production techniques. The BCG vaccine has been used globally to prevent tuberculosis (TB), particularly in children. However, its protective efficacy varies widely depending on the population, environment, and methods of administration. Controlled trials conducted before 1955 reported protective efficacy rates ranging from 56% to 80%. Later studies, including case-control studies, showed efficacy rates ranging from 0% to 80%. In children, the vaccine has demonstrated efficacy rates of 52% to 100% for preventing severe forms of TB, such as tuberculous meningitis and miliary TB, and 2% to 80% for pulmonary TB. However, its efficacy in adolescents and adults, particularly for pulmonary TB, remains inconsistent and unclear. The largest controlled trial of BCG vaccination, conducted in southern India between 1968 and 1971, found no protective efficacy in either children or adults five years after vaccination. A follow-up 15 years later showed a 17% protective efficacy in those vaccinated as children, but no efficacy in those vaccinated as adolescents or adults. These findings highlight the variability in BCG vaccine efficacy and the challenges in determining its role in TB prevention. Meta-analyses of clinical trials and case-control studies have attempted to summarize the vaccine's efficacy. One meta-analysis of 10 clinical trials and 8 case-control studies reported an 86% protective effect against meningitis and miliary TB in children and a 75% effect in case-control studies. However, variability in efficacy rates for pulmonary TB precluded a definitive summary estimate. Another meta-analysis, which included 14 clinical trials and 12 case-control studies, estimated an overall protective effect of 51% in clinical trials and 50% in case-control studies. These analyses also found higher efficacy rates in populations vaccinated during childhood compared to those vaccinated at older ages. The safety of the BCG vaccine is generally well-established, with serious or long-term complications being rare. Common local adverse effects include axillary or cervical lymphadenopathy, induration, pustule formation at the injection site, and permanent scarring. Severe local reactions, such as ulceration, suppurative lymphadenitis, and caseous lesions, may occur but are uncommon. Disseminated BCG infection, though rare, is the most serious complication and is more likely in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with HIV infection. BCG osteitis, affecting the epiphyses of long bones, has been reported in some cases, with an incidence of 1 to 4 cases per million vaccinees in certain regions. The vaccine's safety in HIV-infected individuals has not been fully determined, and there is concern about the risk of disseminated BCG disease in this population. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends BCG vaccination for asymptomatic HIV-infected children in high TB prevalence settings but advises against its use in symptomatic HIV-infected individuals or those at minimal risk of TB infection. BCG vaccination can induce tuberculin reactivity, which may persist for up to 10 years after vaccination in the absence of TB exposure. However, the size of the tuberculin skin test reaction does not reliably predict protection against TB or distinguish between reactions caused by BCG vaccination and those caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. In summary, while the BCG vaccine has been widely used and has demonstrated efficacy in preventing severe TB in children, its role in preventing pulmonary TB in adolescents and adults remains uncertain. Its use in the United States is limited to specific high-risk populations, and it is not recommended for routine TB control or immunization programs.
